title: Anthropic quietly pitches Congress a frontier AI bill that would set a very high bar for model suspensions
subtitle: A confidential draft seen by Politico would let a single federal judge halt a frontier model — but only if regulators show a foreseeable risk of more than $1 billion in damages or 50 serious injuries or deaths.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: Anthropic has given US lawmakers a confidential draft bill that would create a federal process to block the release or use of frontier AI models — but only when the risk is both imminent and severe. Politico first reported the draft on October 16, citing three people familiar with the effort and a copy of the text. Under the proposal, the Commerce Department would petition a single judge of the US District Court for the District of Columbia, who could suspend a model only if the risk meets a high threshold: foreseeable damages above $1 billion, or more than 50 people seriously injured or killed. The risk must originate in a biological weapon, a cyberattack, or a model evading its developer's own controls. Other agencies would be barred from halting development or use on their own authority.

The design is the point. By routing all suspension power through one court and one monetary-or-fatality threshold, Anthropic is proposing a federal regime that would preempt the patchwork of state-level AI laws now taking shape — California's SB 53 is the closest existing analogue. The draft also formalizes a role for independent evaluators registered with Commerce, who would periodically assess labs and their frontier models and have to flag imminent risks within 72 hours. An Anthropic spokesperson said the text reflects the company's Advanced AI Framework, which it has been promoting to federal and state lawmakers since June.

This is the first time a frontier lab has written and shopped its own federal AI bill at this level of detail. The debate it opens is familiar: whether to concentrate oversight in one court with a high evidentiary bar, which gives labs predictability, or to let agencies and states move faster when a specific harm appears. Congress is out of session and has still not passed a federal AI law, so no vote is imminent. The draft is better read as a template that will shape whatever bill does land.

A note for learners: when a company lobbies for a specific regulatory structure, read the thresholds carefully. '$1 billion in damages or 50 serious injuries' sounds precise, but each term is a drafting choice — who counts the damages, over what time window, with what counterfactual. Those definitions are where a bill either bites or becomes decorative.
